entries.message: You picked grandmother, mixing up abuelo and abuela. Abuelo means grandfather, abuela means grandmother — the -o and -a endings tell you the gender of the person being described.
You picked green eyes and grey hair, muddling marrones with verde and blanco with gris. Marrones means brown and blanco means white, so check each colour word carefully.
You picked blonde, confusing rubio (blonde) with blanco (white). Here el pelo blanco specifically means white hair, often used to describe older people like grandparents.
You picked alto y trabajador because those look like the 'normal' adjective forms. But madre is feminine, so both adjectives need the feminine -a ending: alta y trabajadora.
You picked alta y trabajador, fixing only one adjective. Since madre is feminine, every adjective describing her needs to agree, so trabajador must become trabajadora too.
You picked está alta y trabajadora, using estar for a permanent characteristic. Describing someone's personality or lasting traits like height and work ethic needs ser, not estar.
You picked this because 'nos llevamos' looks like it could mean 'I get on with him', but 'nos' means 'we', not 'I...him'. The whole sentence is about a shared 'we' relationship.
You picked this because 'común' looks like 'common' as in ordinary, but 'en común' here means 'in common' (shared interests), not that the people themselves are common.
You picked this because it starts with 'En mi' like the target phrase, but 'en mi casa' means 'in my house', not an opinion phrase like 'in my view'.
You picked this because it also expresses a personal feeling, but 'me gusta mucho' means 'I like it a lot', not 'in my view', which needs 'a mi modo de ver'.

You picked this because it reads like a single event in the past. But 'desde hace veinte años' shows an ongoing state, so it means they have been married for twenty years, not that the wedding happened then.
You picked this by confusing 'casados' (married) with divorce. 'Casados' actually describes their marital status as married, so the sentence is about them being married, not divorced.
You picked this because 'viviré' looks similar to 'viviría' and both relate to future time. But the future ending is '-é', while the conditional uses '-ía', giving 'viviría' for 'would live'.
You picked this thinking of a completed past action, but 'viví' is the preterite (I lived). The conditional needs the '-ía' ending attached to the infinitive, making it 'viviría' for 'would live'.
You picked 'must' because deber can mean 'must'. But debería is the conditional form, softer than debo, so it translates as 'should', not the stronger 'must'.
You picked 'can' by mixing up deber with poder. Poder means 'can/to be able to', while deber(ía) expresses obligation or advice, giving 'should' here.
You picked 'Debo como' because como looks like a normal verb form you know. But after a modal verb like debo, Spanish needs an infinitive, so comer is required, not como.
You picked 'Debo comiendo' by treating it like an -ing construction. Spanish doesn't pair modal verbs with gerunds this way; debo must be followed by the infinitive comer.

You picked cooked because cené looks similar to cociné, and riquísimo can sound negative. Actually cené means 'I had for dinner' and riquísimo means really delicious, so the meal was eaten and enjoyed, not cooked or disgusting.

You picked breakfast, maybe muddling cené (dinner) with desayuné (breakfast), and horrible instead of riquísimo. Remember cené means 'I dined' and riquísimo is a strong positive word meaning really delicious.
You picked today with salad, mixing up ayer (yesterday) with hoy (today) and patatas fritas (chips) with salad. Ayer signals past tense, and cené fish specifically with chips, not salad.
You picked gusta because it's the form you see most often, but gustar agrees with what's liked. Since patatas fritas is plural, you need gustan to match, giving Me gustan las patatas fritas.

You picked gustas, treating gustar like a normal verb agreeing with the person speaking. Actually gustar agrees with the thing liked, not the speaker, so plural patatas fritas needs gustan, not gustas.
You picked this because '¿Qué le pasa?' sounds like it's asking about location. Actually 'dónde te duele' asks where it hurts; 'qué le pasa' asks generally what's wrong.
You went for this thinking of '¿Cómo te sientes?', which does mean how you're feeling. But '¿Qué le pasa?' is asking what's wrong, not how someone feels.
You used 'duelen' thinking of plural agreement, but 'garganta' is singular, so it needs 'duele'. Remember the verb agrees with the body part, not with 'me'.
You used 'dolor' here, but that's the noun for pain, not a verb. To say something hurts you need the verb 'duele', giving 'me duele la garganta'.
You picked this because peligroso looks a bit like it could mean painful, and you read hay riesgo as no risk. Peligroso means dangerous, and hay riesgo de means there IS a risk of cancer.
You picked this because peligroso and popular sound vaguely similar, and cáncer got swapped for colds. Actually peligroso means dangerous, and cáncer just means cancer, not resfriado.
You picked this because you read hay riesgo as if it said no risk. Actually hay riesgo de cáncer means there IS a risk of cancer, with no negative word present.
You picked this because imposible looks similar to importante at a glance. But imposible means impossible, not important, so this sentence says it's impossible to avoid drugs.
You picked this because interesante and importante share letters and both sound like positive judgements. Interesante actually means interesting, not important, so the meaning changes.
You picked this because you focused on drogas and missed that tomar means to take, not to avoid. Evitar means avoid, so tomar gives the opposite meaning here.
You picked 'less fun' because menos and más can blur together. But más divertida means more fun, so ICT comes out ahead of Geography, not behind it.
You picked 'as fun as' because that's how comparisons often sound. But más...que signals a clear comparison of degree, not equality, so it means more fun than, not equally fun.
You picked Geography as the winner by reading the sentence back to front. Informática is the subject at the start, so ICT is the one being described as more fun.
You picked gusta because it sounds simpler, but matemáticas is plural, so the verb must agree as gustan, matching what you don't like.
You picked putting nada at the end because English puts 'at all' there. In Spanish, nada sits right after the verb, before the thing you dislike, to strengthen the negative.
You picked quarter past because 'cuarto' suggests adding fifteen minutes. But 'menos cuarto' means minus a quarter, so it's quarter to three, not quarter past.
You picked three o'clock because you spotted 'tres' and stopped there. But 'menos cuarto' changes it to quarter to three, so you need to subtract fifteen minutes.
You picked Son la una because 'son' feels like the standard way to say 'it is'. But one o'clock is singular, so Spanish uses 'es la una', not 'son'.
You picked Es las una because 'las' seems to match other times. But 'una' is singular, so it needs the singular article 'la', giving 'es la una'.
You picked university because bachillerato sounds like higher education. Actually bachillerato refers to Spanish A-levels, the school stage before university, so it means I am going to do A-levels.

You picked work since future plans often mention jobs. But hacer el bachillerato specifically means completing school-level qualifications, not starting employment, so it translates as I am going to do A-levels.
You picked trabajé because it looks similar, but that's the preterite past tense meaning I worked. The simple future needs the future ending, giving trabajaré, I will work.
You picked trabajaba thinking of past habitual actions, meaning I used to work. For simple future, add é to the infinitive: trabajaré, meaning I will work.
